cse-2004-cs-70.approach: An implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. Find one falsifying and one satisfying assignment.

steps.title: Try to falsify
steps.body:
Need $(P\vee Q)\to R$ false: $P\vee Q = T$, $R = F$. Take $P=F,\ Q=T,\ R=F$.

Then $P\to(Q\vee R) = F\to T = T$, so the whole formula is $T\to F = F$. **Not valid.**

steps.title: Find a model
steps.body: With $R=T$: $(P\vee Q)\to T = T$, so the formula is $(\ldots)\to T = T$. **Satisfiable.**

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: True for some assignments, false for others: satisfiable but not valid.

pitfalls: Reading $\to$ as associative: the main connective is the middle arrow.

cse-2004-cs-71.approach: Solve two equations, then test the third. A consistent overdetermined 3×2 system with independent columns has exactly one solution.

steps.title: Solve the last two
steps.body: $x - y = 2 \Rightarrow x = y + 2$. Substituting into $x + 3y = 3$: $y + 2 + 3y = 3 \Rightarrow 4y = 1 \Rightarrow y = \tfrac14$, $x = \tfrac94$.

steps.title: Check the first
steps.body: $-x + 5y = -\tfrac94 + \tfrac54 = -\tfrac44 = -1$ ✓.

steps.title: Count solutions
steps.body: The coefficient matrix has rank 2 (rows $(1,-1)$ and $(1,3)$ are independent) and the system is consistent, so the solution $(\tfrac94, \tfrac14)$ is **unique**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Infinite solutions need rank < 2; here rank = 2.
A linear system never has exactly two solutions.

cse-2004-cs-73.approach: A finite poset is a complete lattice iff it has a bottom and a top and every pair has a meet and join. Find what is missing.

steps.title: Top exists, bottom does not

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: A finite lattice is complete, so adding $\{1\}$ alone is **necessary and sufficient**.

cse-2004-cs-76.approach: Entries with no two in a common row or column form a matching; every chosen entry needs its own covering line (König–Egerváry), so the count is at most the number of covering lines a + b.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: Rows and columns are the two sides of a bipartite graph; each non-zero entry $(i,j)$ is an edge. Entries with no two sharing a row or column form a **matching**. The $a$ rows and $b$ columns that cover all non-zero entries form a **vertex cover** of size $a+b$.

steps.title: Bound
steps.body: Each line (row or column) of the cover can contain at most one entry of the matching, and every matching entry lies in some covering line. So the matching has at most $a + b$ entries (König: max matching = min line cover).

steps.title: Why the others fail
steps.body: Example: $a = b = 1$, non-zeros in row 1 and column 1 (a cross). Entries $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ are independent: 2 entries $> \max\{1,1\} = \min\{1,1\} = 1$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Each independent entry consumes a distinct covering line.
The cross example gives 2 > max{1,1}.
$M-a$, $N-b$ count uncovered lines, which hold no non-zeros; unrelated bound.
Fails for the cross example; it would hold only if the non-zeros sat inside an a×b submatrix.

pitfalls: Reading "covered in a rows and b columns" as "inside the a×b intersection" gives min{a,b}; the covering (union) reading is the König setting.
cse-2004-cs-76.verification: Cross example ($a=b=1$, 2 independent entries) confirms A is the only bound valid for every cover.

- Triangle $L,c,B$: $B = 2$.

cse-2004-cs-81.approach: Contrapositive: if G1 ∪ G2 had no cycle it would be a spanning tree, forcing G1 = G2 = that tree and a connected intersection.

steps.title: Assume no cycle
steps.body: $G_1 \cup G_2$ is connected (it contains $G_1$). If it were acyclic it would be a tree $T$ with exactly $|V|-1$ edges.

steps.title: Derive a contradiction
steps.body: $G_1$ and $G_2$ are connected spanning subgraphs of the tree $T$, so each needs $\geq |V|-1$ edges, hence $G_1 = G_2 = T$. Then $G_1 \cap G_2 = T$ is connected — contradiction. So $G_1 \cup G_2$ **must have a cycle**.

steps.title: Kill the other options
steps.body: On $V = \{1,2,3\}$ take $G_1 = \{12, 23\}$, $G_2 = \{13, 23\}$: the intersection $\{23\}$ leaves vertex 1 isolated. The union is a triangle — it has no bridge (kills C). Adding a pendant vertex 4 joined to 3 in both graphs makes 3 a cut vertex (kills A). Two different spanning paths of a 4-cycle give a 2-colourable union (kills D).

An acyclic union would force $G_1 = G_2$, making the intersection connected.

steps.body: $S \to b$ ends with a-count $\equiv 0$; $B \to a$ ends with $2 + 1 \equiv 0$. $A$ has no terminating rule. Hence $N_a(w) \equiv 0 \pmod 3$ for every $w \in L(G)$.
